Chapters

snippet.title: Did You Notice? 12 Rounds, One Change Each
snippet.description:
A 10-minute attention game. 12 rounds in Cella's house. In each round, one thing changes. Spot it before the bell and give yourself a point.

What was your score?

Chapters
0:00 Round 1: the kitchen
0:38 How to play
0:55 Round 2: the plate
1:35 Round 3: the bedroom
2:15 Round 4: the stairs
2:55 Round 5: the moon
3:35 Round 6: the door
4:15 Why is this so hard?
5:00 Round 7: the table
5:40 Round 8: the blanket
6:20 Round 9: the clock
7:00 Round 10: the stars
7:40 Round 11: Cella
8:20 Round 12: the door, again
9:10 Your score
9:40 Where this happens every day
10:15 The idea behind the game

The idea behind the game: "change blindness". When something changes in a part of a scene we are not paying attention to, we often miss it, even when the change is big.
Simons, D. J., & Levin, D. T. (1998). Failure to detect changes to people during a real-world interaction. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 5(4), 644-649. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03208840
Rensink, R. A., O'Regan, J. K., & Clark, J. J. (1997). To see or not to see: The need for attention to perceive changes in scenes. Psychological Science, 8(5), 368-373. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.1997.tb00427.x
Simons, D. J., Franconeri, S. L., & Reimer, R. L. (2000). Change blindness in the absence of a visual disruption. Perception, 29(10), 1143-1154. https://doi.org/10.1068/p3104

Made with code and Claude. Music composed with code by NAOS, no samples; one short sound effect from our own library.
Closer to yourself.

snippet.title: Things to Do Instead of Scrolling: Cella Tries 12
snippet.description:
One day in Cella's house. Twelve times she reaches for her phone for no reason. Twelve times she does something else, and we time it. At the end she keeps her three favorites.

What would you do instead?

Chapters
0:00 She reaches for the phone
0:22 How this works
0:42 1. A glass of water
1:17 2. Water the plant
1:52 3. Look out the window
2:27 4. Put one thing back
3:02 5. Lunch with no phone
3:37 6. Fold the blanket
4:12 Halfway: why deciding first helps
5:12 7. Use the phone on purpose
5:47 8. Read one page (it didn't work)
6:27 9. Make tea
7:02 10. Knock on Rina's door
7:37 11. Find the moon
8:12 12. Nothing at all
9:22 The three she keeps
9:50 Your turn

The idea in the middle comes from research on "if-then plans": deciding in advance what you will do when a certain moment comes ("If I reach for my phone with no reason, then I water the plant"). Across many studies (94 independent tests in the 2006 review), people who made plans like this followed through on what they meant to do more often than people who only had the goal, on average; not everyone, and not every time.
Gollwitzer, P. M. (1999). Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans. American Psychologist, 54(7), 493-503. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.54.7.493
Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69-119. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(06)38002-1

Made with code and Claude. Narration by the NAOS voice (ElevenLabs). Music composed with code by NAOS. Sounds from our own library.
Closer to yourself.

snippet.title: 66 Days in the House: How a Habit Forms
snippet.description:
Cella tries one small thing: a glass of water right after she gets up. Same place, same moment, every day. Each night she answers one question, from 1 to 7: "Did I do it without thinking?" We watch the curve on her fridge for 66 days, including the days she forgets, and Cella tells it in her own voice.

Then she reads the real study behind the number 66 out loud: what the researchers did, what they found, what nobody knows yet, and why 66 is a middle number.

What small thing would you try for 66 days?

Chapters
0:00 Day 66
0:35 The plan
1:40 Days 1 to 7: remembering
5:00 Day 8
5:15 Day 9: she forgot
6:00 Days 10 to 13
6:30 Day 14: a different kitchen
7:15 Days 15 to 20
7:50 Day 21: nothing special
8:30 Days 22 and 23: forgot again
9:30 Days 24 to 35: less effort
11:45 Days 36 to 65: the flat part
13:10 Day 66
14:02 Why 66 days? The study
15:26 18 to 254 days
16:58 Three curves
17:54 Your turn

The study: about 96 volunteers each chose one new eating, drinking or activity behavior to do every day in the same context (for example, after breakfast) for 12 weeks, and answered questions every day about how automatic it felt (p. 998). 82 gave enough data. Their answers formed a clear curve for 39 of the 82. Among those 39, the median time to reach near their highest level of automaticity was 66 days, and the range was 18 to 254 days (p. 1002). The study lasted 84 days, so the longer numbers are estimates from each person's curve. People who chose exercise tended to take longer than people who chose eating or drinking, but the groups were small and the difference was not firm. Missing one day did not materially change the process (p. 1006). People who did the behavior more consistently had clearer curves.
Cella's numbers are part of the story, not data.
Lally, P., van Jaarsveld, C. H. M., Potts, H. W. W., & Wardle, J. (2010). How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 40(6), 998-1009. https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.674

snippet.title: Live Commentary: Someone Overthinks a Text That Says "ok"
snippet.description:
Live from the living room: Cella's friend Sam answered her text with "ok". Two letters, lowercase, no period. Two commentators call the next 41 minutes.

For the friend who reads one "ok" nine times.

Chapters
0:00 Kickoff: the "ok"
0:28 The first read
1:06 The investigation
1:38 The drafts
2:14 Halftime: what a text can't carry
3:53 The guess tree
4:29 The question
5:08 The replay, from Sam's side
5:38 Also tonight
5:54 Full time

The idea at halftime comes from a set of studies on email by Justin Kruger, Nicholas Epley and colleagues. College students sent short messages meant to sound sarcastic or serious. The writers were too confident the tone would come through, and the readers were too confident they had read it right. In one study, readers of email guessed the tone about as well as chance, while feeling almost as sure as people who heard it spoken. In another, friends did no better than strangers. These were emails between college students, in a paper from 2005, and the studies did not test what happens when someone simply asks.
Kruger, J., Epley, N., Parker, J., & Ng, Z.-W. (2005). Egocentrism over e-mail: Can we communicate as well as we think? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 89(6), 925-936. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.89.6.925

One idea behind the ending comes from research on conversations: after talking with someone new, people tend to underestimate how much the other person liked them. snippet.title: Live Commentary: Someone Tries to Leave the Party
snippet.description:
Live from the living room: Cella wants to go home. The door is six meters away. Two commentators call every move.

For the friend who says goodbye three times.

Chapters
0:00 Kickoff
0:22 "I should go"
1:03 "Already?"
1:43 The coat
2:33 The goodbye round
3:25 Halftime: why leaving takes so long
5:11 The question at the door
5:46 The goal
6:10 The replay
6:43 Also tonight
6:55 Full time

The idea at halftime comes from a study by Adam Mastroianni and colleagues at Harvard. More than 800 people described their last conversation, and 252 strangers talked in pairs in a lab for as long as they liked, up to 45 minutes. In the lab, both people got the ending they wanted in 2 of 126 conversations; in almost half, both wanted to stop earlier; and people's guesses about when the other wanted to stop were off by about nine minutes. These were conversations between two people, not parties, and the study did not test what happens when someone simply says it.
Mastroianni, A. M., Gilbert, D. T., Cooney, G., & Wilson, T. D. (2021). Do conversations end when people want them to? PNAS, 118(10), e2011809118. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2011809118

snippet.title: Why We Clean the Kitchen Instead of Answering One Email
snippet.description:
For the friend with one email they've been avoiding since Monday.

Cella has one email to answer. By Thursday night, the kitchen has never been cleaner. Why do people put off one small task by doing everything else? Two voices go back and forth between Cella's week and the research: a lab experiment with a candle, a study that followed students through a term, a large review of procrastination research, and what the numbers say about perfectionism. Each day of Cella's week brings a different kind of unpleasant, and one thing she tries. The four kinds are this video's way of sorting it; each one leans on different research, named below.

Which of the four did your task have? And what's the task?

Chapters
0:00 One email
0:58 The feel-better trade
1:54 The candle experiment
3:51 What made this email different
4:13 Monday: boring
5:27 Tuesday: too big
6:36 Wednesday: being judged
8:03 Thursday: no next step, and who pays
10:05 Friday: the first step
10:47 What the studies can't say

The studies:
Sirois & Pychyl (2013) review research arguing that putting a task off is often a way to repair mood in the short term, with the cost landing on the "future self".
Tice, Bratslavsky & Baumeister (2001, Study 3): 88 college students had 15 minutes to practice for a math test. Those in a bad mood, with fun things in the room, who believed their mood could change, spent on average 13.7 of the 15 minutes on other things; those told a candle had "frozen" their mood, 5.7. One lab study; it measured practice time, not a real deadline.
Tice & Baumeister (1997): two studies, 44 students and then about 60, in one course. Students who tended to put things off reported less stress early in the term, more near the end, and got lower grades. Self-reported and correlational.
Steel (2007): a meta-analysis of 691 correlations. Task aversiveness was one of the strongest and most consistent predictors of putting things off (r = 0.40), with boredom standing out among its parts. Perfectionism showed almost no link (r = -0.03). The fear-of-failure group, which in this review includes socially prescribed perfectionism (feeling that others expect perfection), showed a weak one (r = 0.18, for the whole group). The review also suggests "pairing" and closer goals, and cites an older observation (Silver, 1974) that more decision points go with more delay. These are correlations: they show what tends to come together.
Sirois, Molnar & Hirsch (2017): a meta-analysis that split perfectionism in two. High personal standards went with slightly less putting off (r = -0.22); worry about mistakes and others' judgment with slightly more (r = 0.23).
What Cella tries is her own.

Sirois, F., & Pychyl, T. (2013). Procrastination and the priority of short-term mood regulation: Consequences for future self. Social and Personality Psychology Compass, 7(2), 115-127.
Tice, D. M., Bratslavsky, E., & Baumeister, R. F. (2001). Emotional distress regulation takes precedence over impulse control: If you feel bad, do it! Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 80(1), 53-67.
Tice, D. M., & Baumeister, R. F. (1997). Longitudinal study of procrastination, performance, stress, and health: The costs and benefits of dawdling. Psychological Science, 8(6), 454-458.
Steel, P. (2007). The nature of procrastination: A meta-analytic and theoretical review of quintessential self-regulatory failure. Psychological Bulletin, 133(1), 65-94.
Sirois, F. M., Molnar, D. S., & Hirsch, J. K. (2017). A meta-analytic and conceptual update on the associations between procrastination and multidimensional perfectionism. European Journal of Personality, 31(2), 137-159.

Made with code and Claude. Music composed with code by NAOS. Voices by ElevenLabs.
